newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine provinces take first steps into bond mkt.
newsitem.headline: Argentine provinces take first steps into bond mkt.

text.p: Argentina's provinces, emboldened by improving economic conditions and stronger fiscal balance sheets, are going where they have never gone before: the international capital markets.

More and more of the country's provinces are jumping on the bandwagon to issue bonds, wanting to follow on the coattails of the central government's recent successes in selling debt overseas at lower rates.
"The provinces have discovered that issuing bonds is a good way to diversify their debt," said Silvia Hoevel, an underwriter at Argentina's Banco Rio.

A host of provinces are queuing up. Not only are they entering the markets for the first time, but they are also coming up with novel debt structures, heralding a mini-boom in new forms of securitization in Argentina.

The relatively wealthy Mendoza paved the way in August, issuing $150 million of debentures due 2002, collateralized with royalties from five oil concessions in the province. The lead manager was Lehman Brothers.
Mendoza is now thinking of issuing a new bond guaranteed by agricultural credits.

Argentina's southernmost province, Tierra del Fuego, hopes to top the Mendoza oil bond with a $160 million note, to be collateralized with oil and gas royalties. Rothschild will be the global co-ordinator. Neuquen, another oil-rich province,
has issued $63 million in bonds due March 2001 also guaranteed by oil and gas royalties.
The governor of Cordoba said this week his province also wants to join the party, to issue $200 million next year as soon as Standard & Poor's gives it a credit rating.

Part of the keenness by the provinces to issue debt may be motivated by the obvious interest in business by underwriters. This week U.S. investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette made an offer to lead manage issues worth $300 million by Chaco province before legislation to go ahead with such issues has even been approved.
"The provinces are learning from the nation," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings, referring to the country's increasing experience in world capital markets.

Sharp recent gains in Argentina's bond prices thanks to low U.S. yields and high international liquidity levels are helping the provinces venture into the markets. "The markets are accepting the provinces' risk," said Hoevel of Banco Rio.
One of the most important reasons the provinces are now in a position to enter the markets is the accumulated effects of economic reforms led by Peronist President Carlos Menem.

The privatization drive and cuts in spending introduced since 1991 have obliged the regions to sell off state banks, institutions that in the past often served as easy providers of credit to cash-hungry provinces.
With that avenue of credit no longer open, new forms of borrowing have become necessary.
The sharp recession in 1995 caused by the devaluation of the Mexican peso did much of the rest of the job, forcing the provinces to finish the job of improving their finances.

"Many remaining provinces that had avoided all intentions to make reforms during the boom (from 1991 to 1994) had no choice but to introduce adjustments and transformations during the recession," said consultants M&S in a recent report.

"The provinces will have more resources next year and will be major winners from macroeconomic improvements," added M&S, saying next year's anticipated recovery would give them a much firmer base to attract buyers in search of higher yield.
